structure.title: Prologue and parodos · A household hears its mistress
structure.text: The Nurse explains Jason's new marriage while Medea cries out indoors. Her children are onstage before she is. The gap between what servants fear and what their mistress will actually do holds the opening together.

structure.title: First to third episodes · One day to leave Corinth
structure.text: Creon orders Medea into exile. She extracts a delay, argues with Jason and obtains a promise from a passing king. The apparent digressions are practical necessities for a woman who must find out how much time and shelter she has.

structure.title: Fourth episode · A plan brought into the house
structure.text: Once Medea has secured a future beyond Corinth, the question becomes what she can bring herself to do before leaving. The children have errands to run in a quarrel whose meaning they cannot understand.

people.name: Medea and Jason
people.text: Her help made his exploits possible. His new marriage offers a connection to local royalty. Both can tell a coherent story about who has benefited the other, and neither accepts the other's account of their debt.

people.name: The Corinthian women
people.text: The chorus can recognise the danger of a husband's betrayal from ordinary life. Sympathy gives Medea listeners. Its limits become painfully important when she asks them to keep silent.

context.title: A foreign wife facing exile
context.text: Medea left her own family to follow Jason. When he changes households, she has neither an independent position in Corinth nor relatives nearby to take her in. Securing a sworn promise of refuge matters as much as winning an argument.

notice.text: Whose language does she speak in each interview?
notice.why: Medea can sound like a neighbour addressing women, a mother begging a father, or a strategist examining an alliance. Each listener hears a different portion of what she knows.

notice.text: Follow the children in and out of the doorway.
notice.why: While adults debate their prospects, they carry objects, obey instructions and return home. These small movements onstage let the audience measure a parent's argument against the lives it concerns.

opening: Jason is leaving Medea to marry a princess and explains that the arrangement will benefit everyone. Medea has abandoned her country, betrayed her family, and borne his children; he would like her to understand the advantages of his new position. Euripides lets her answer with a clarity that makes his self-justification collapse. Then the woman whose grievance is so easy to recognise begins considering what she can still do with it. Her intelligence remains formidable as her intentions become harder to bear.
